procedural_history.originating_court: West Bengal First Special Court at Alipore
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated November 20, 1953, convicting the appellant under s. 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and under s. 161 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant unsuccessfully appealed to the High Court against his conviction and sentence. The High Court then certified the case under Art. 134(1)(c) of the Constitution as fit for appeal to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the High Court certified the case as fit for appeal, specifically on the ground that the sanction accorded in the case was not a valid sanction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sanction accorded for the prosecution of the appellant was a valid sanction.

facts: The sanction document (Ex. 6) stated the specific facts of the case: the appellant allegedly accepted a Rs. 100 bribe on May 12, 1952, for the speedy settlement of claim cases.
The document also explicitly stated that the sanctioning officer, Mr. Bokil, had applied his mind to the facts and was satisfied that prosecution was in the interests of justice.
In his testimony, Mr. Bokil stated that before granting sanction, he "went through all relevant papers" and was satisfied that the appellant should be prosecuted.
In cross-examination, Mr. Bokil admitted that the sanction document was prepared by the police and that he did not call for office records or investigate the truth of the allegations himself.
law: The sanctioning authority is not required to judge the truth of the allegations made against the accused.
The authority's duty is to review the material placed before them and decide if it is necessary in the ends of justice to accord sanction for prosecution.
The fact that a sanction document is drafted by the police does not automatically invalidate it, provided the sanctioning authority applies their mind to the case materials before signing.
application: The Court considered Mr. Bokil's testimony and the sanction document together.

It found that Mr. Bokil's statement that he reviewed all relevant papers before signing was credible, despite the document being drafted by the police. The Court found it "inconceivable" that a high-ranking officer would sign such a document blindly.

The Court reasoned that Mr. Bokil's admission that he did not investigate the truth of the case was not detrimental, as this was not his role. His responsibility was to determine if there was sufficient material to warrant a prosecution, which the papers placed before him provided.
The Court concluded that the sanction document itself contained all the necessary facts, and Mr. Bokil's evidence confirmed he had applied his mind to those facts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the sanction was valid. It found that the sanctioning officer had applied his mind to the relevant materials before him, which is the essential requirement for a valid sanction, even if he did not personally investigate the truth of the allegations or draft the sanction order himself. Therefore, the appellant's contention was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sanction accorded for the prosecution of the appellant was a valid sanction.
appellant_arguments: The sanction was invalid because the sanctioning authority, Mr. Bokil, had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case.
This was evidenced by Mr. Bokil's statements in cross-examination where he admitted that the sanction document was prepared by the police and put before him.
Mr. Bokil also admitted that he did not call for any records from his office or investigate the truth of the allegations, which showed he granted the sanction mechanically.
The appellant cited the case of Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King in support of this submission.
respondent_arguments: The sanction was valid as established by the sanction document (Ex. 6) and the evidence of the sanctioning authority, Mr. Bokil.
The sanction document on its face clearly stated the facts constituting the offence and that Mr. Bokil had applied his mind to the case.
In his examination-in-chief, Mr. Bokil testified that he had gone through all the relevant papers and was satisfied that prosecution was in the interests of justice.

It was not the duty of the sanctioning authority to judge the truth of the allegations by calling for records or conducting an investigation; his role was to decide if the materials placed before him warranted a prosecution.

cases.case_name: Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King
cases.principle: The case was referred to for the essentials of a valid sanction for prosecution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A valid sanction for the prosecution of a public servant requires the sanctioning authority to apply their mind to the materials placed before them to decide if prosecution is necessary; it is not required for the authority to conduct an independent investigation to judge the truth of the allegations before granting the sanction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When the sanction document (Exhibit 6) and the evidence of the sanctioning authority, Mr. Bokil, are scrutinized and read together, there is little doubt that the sanction was valid. The sanction on its face clearly states the facts constituting the offence and that the authority had applied his mind, and this is supported by his testimony that he went through all the relevant papers and was satisfied that prosecution was in the interests of justice.
legal_tests_applied: A sanction is valid if the sanctioning authority has applied their mind to the facts and circumstances of the case to determine if a prosecution is warranted, as established by the sanction document itself and the evidence of the authority.
The precedent set in Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King, which requires the sanctioning authority to be aware of the facts of the case before granting sanction.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's reliance on Mr. Bokil's cross-examination, where he admitted the police prepared the sanction document, was insufficient to invalidate the sanction when viewed against his examination-in-chief and the contents of the document itself.

The argument that Mr. Bokil failed to apply his mind because he did not call for office records or investigate the truth of the allegations was rejected, as the court held it was not the sanctioning authority's duty to judge the truth of the allegations.

The appellant's reliance on the precedent in Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King was misplaced, as the court found that the sanction in this case was in keeping with, and did not conflict with, the principles laid down in that case.
why_respondent_won: The sanction document (Exhibit 6) on its face was clear and sufficient, stating all the necessary facts of the case and expressly mentioning that the sanctioning authority had applied his mind and was satisfied that prosecution was in the interests of justice.

The testimony of the sanctioning authority, Mr. Bokil, in his examination-in-chief, confirmed that he had reviewed all relevant papers placed before him and was satisfied that a prosecution should be initiated.

The court clarified the role of the sanctioning authority, stating that their duty is not to conduct an independent investigation or judge the truth of the allegations, but to decide if the materials placed before them warrant a prosecution. Mr. Bokil fulfilled this duty.
